\chapter{Two Tamils}
\label{ch:ta-two-tamils}
\hlchaptermodality{81}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say why written Tamil and spoken Tamil differ, and move between them.}

Complete TA-C81-which-tamil and say three joining words in both forms.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āṉāl / āṉā]{\ta{ஆனால்} / \ta{ஆனா} — the two Tamils}

\label{lesson:TA-C81-two-tamils}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}. Then ask a shopkeeper the price.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: one language, two forms, and everybody uses both}]
Something has been happening quietly in the last eight chapters, and it is time it was said plainly.

Tamil comes in two forms. One is written — in books, on signs, in the news. The other is spoken — at home, in a shop, on a bus. They are not an accent apart. Words differ, and endings differ, and a page of one is not a recording of the other.

Every Tamil speaker uses both and knows which is which. Nobody chooses one and abandons the other.

You have already met three pairs, one per chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{spoken} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}} & \textbf{\ta{ஆனா}} \\
\textbf{\ta{ஏனென்றால்}} & \textbf{\ta{ஏன்னா}} \\
\textbf{\ta{என்று}} & \textbf{-\ta{ன்னு}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is not a coincidence of these particular words. Joining words are where the split shows most, because they are said constantly and worn down fastest — the same reason an English speaker says \emph{cos} far more often than \emph{because}.

It reaches ordinary words too: \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, the written \emph{today}, is \textbf{\ta{இன்னிக்கி}} in speech.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The single most important fact about Tamil, and a reason the last eight chapters gave you two forms of everything.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āṉāl}, then \emph{āṉā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}, then \emph{ēṉṉā}
  \item \emph{Listen:} for the piece that is dropped each time — a closing consonant
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}, then ask \emph{vilai evvaḷavu?}, then say both forms of \emph{but}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{alladu} and \emph{-um pōdu} — two distances back — then say which of the two Tamils each one belongs to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does a Tamil speaker pick one of the two forms and keep to it? (\textbf{No — everyone uses both, in different places.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṉṟu / -ṉṉu]{\ta{என்று} / -\ta{ன்னு} — which one you are being taught}

\label{lesson:TA-C81-which-tamil}



\begin{quote}
Ask a price. Then say \emph{but} twice — the written way, then the spoken way.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: the headword is the written one, on purpose}]
In every lesson of this book, the big word at the top is the \textbf{written} form, and the spoken clip is named beside it in the text. That choice is worth explaining, because it is not obvious.

The written form is the one on the page you will read, the sign you will pass and the form your dictionary will list. It is also understood everywhere Tamil is spoken, which no single spoken variety is.

And it runs one way. From \textbf{\ta{என்று}} you can predict \textbf{-\ta{ன்னு}}; from \textbf{-\ta{ன்னு}} alone you could not have rebuilt \textbf{\ta{என்று}}. Learn the longer one and the shorter one comes free.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ta{சரி}\textquotedblright{} \ta{என்று} \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.} — written
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ta{சரி}\textquotedblright{}\ta{ன்னு} \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.} — spoken
\end{quote}

Same sentence. The quotation does not move, the verb does not move; the joining word shrinks onto the word in front of it.

So: say either. Expect to \textbf{hear} the clipped one nearly always, and read the full one nearly always.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You know which Tamil is in front of you, and you can get from one to the other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{}-ṉṉu solluṅgaḷ}
  \item \emph{Convert:} take \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl} and say the clip; take \emph{ēṉṉā} and rebuild the full word
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}, then ask \emph{vilai evvaḷavu?}, then say both forms of the quotation line
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{mēlē}, read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}} and say \emph{maṟṟadu} — three distances back — then say which of the two Tamils each one belongs to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does this book put the written form at the top? (\textbf{Because the spoken form follows from it, and not the other way round.})
\end{tcolorbox}
